anchor: Lines on the loss of the
title: Title and occasion
short: Written within days of the sinking of RMS Titanic (15 April 1912) and first printed for a charity matinée in aid of the disaster fund.
body: The White Star liner Titanic, advertised as practically unsinkable, struck an iceberg on her maiden voyage and sank on 15 April 1912 with the loss of some 1,500 lives. Hardy dated his poem 24 April 1912, and it was first printed in the souvenir programme of the 'Dramatic and Operatic Matinée in Aid of the Titanic Disaster Fund' at the Royal Opera House, Covent Garden, on 14 May 1912, in a shorter early form of thirty lines (the final text has thirty-three), under the headnote 'Improvised on the Loss of the Titanic'. It was revised and collected in Satires of Circumstance (1914). For a charity occasion the poem is strikingly cold: it names no victim and offers no consolation, and critics have long debated whether it is a sermon on vanity or a detached cosmic fable (see the 'Immanent Will' note).

title: Twain (title) and twin halves
greek: OE twēgen; Lat. convergere, 'to incline together'
short: The title's 'Twain' (archaic 'two') becomes the 'twin halves' of l. 30: ship and iceberg as a destined pair.
body: 'Twain' (Old English twā / twēgen) survived by 1912 mainly in elevated, biblical and proverbial use; its best-known occurrence is the marriage text 'they twain shall be one flesh' (Matthew 19:5), which the poem's language of 'mate', 'intimate welding' and 'consummation' grimly echoes. 'Convergence' is geometric and scientific: two lines of travel meeting at a point, the paths 'coincident' of st. X. The title therefore yokes a Latinate, almost technical noun to an archaic, ceremonial one, the same blend of registers that marks the whole poem. Its 'twain' returns as 'twin halves': two parts of one whole, recalling the myth in Plato's Symposium of lovers as severed halves seeking reunion, though whether Hardy intended that echo is uncertain.

anchor: IN a solitude of the sea
title: Stanza form
short: Eleven triplet-rhymed tercets: two short trimeter lines and a long hexameter, a shape often compared to a ship or an iceberg.
body: Each stanza rhymes aaa, with two short lines (roughly trimeter) followed by a long line of six stresses. Readers have seen the printed shape as visual mimesis, the long third line as the hull or the submerged bulk of the iceberg, with more below the surface than above. The single sustained rhyme makes each stanza close with a heavy, inevitable click. The poem also divides in two: stanzas I–V show the wreck on the sea-floor; stanzas VI–XI turn back in time to the parallel 'growth' of ship and ice, a structural convergence that mirrors the subject. Some readers have also made something of the odd number of stanzas (eleven), though this is interpretive rather than documented.

sources.cite: 'The Convergence of the Twain', Wikipedia (summarising Childs, Baldick and Davie)
Samuel Hynes, ed., The Complete Poetical Works of Thomas Hardy, vol. 2 (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1984), text and notes for the poem

title: the Pride of Life
short: From 1 John 2:16, where 'the pride of life' is one of the three worldly lusts that are 'not of the Father'.
body: The capitalised phrase quotes the King James Bible: 'For all that is in the world, the lust of the flesh, and the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life, is not of the Father, but is of the world' (1 John 2:16). Hardy makes it almost an allegorical person, the vainglory that 'planned her'. The biblical frame governs stanzas I–V, which itemise worldly vanities (luxury fittings, mirrors, jewels) now rendered useless. Note, though, that Hardy does not adopt the Epistle's theology: the agent of retribution later in the poem is not a judging God but the impersonal Immanent Will.

sources.cite: Bible (KJV), 1 John 2:16

title: stilly couches
short: 'Stilly' is a poetic form of 'quietly'; 'couches' means lies down, as an animal in its lair or a body on a bed.
body: 'Stilly' (adverb, 'silently, calmly') is an old poetic word, familiar from Thomas Moore's 'Oft in the stilly night'. 'Couch' as an intransitive verb means to lie down or lie hidden, used of beasts in a den and of sleepers or the dead. The inverted syntax ('couches she') and the feminine pronoun conventional for ships prepare for the poem's later treatment of the liner as a bride. The calm verb also contrasts ironically with the violence of the sinking, which the poem never describes.

title: salamandrine fires
short: The ship's furnaces are likened to the salamander, the creature fabled to live in fire.
body: Ancient natural history held that the salamander could live in, or even quench, fire (Aristotle, Historia animalium 5.19; Pliny, Natural History 10.86). Hardy's adjective makes the stokeholds of the steamship a home of elemental fire, now drowned in its opposite element: the 'pyres' of the boilers are 'late' (former) and cold currents pass through them. The word 'pyres' also hints at funeral fires, a quiet reminder of the dead the poem otherwise leaves unmentioned.

title: thrid
short: Archaic variant of 'thread': the currents pass through the steel chambers as a thread through a needle's eye.
body: 'Thrid' is an old by-form of the verb 'thread', meaning to pass through a narrow or intricate way; the OED records it chiefly in literary use from the sixteenth century on. The chambers once full of fire are now threaded by currents that 'turn to rhythmic tidal lyres', that is, the flowing water plays on the hull's openings like wind on the strings of a lyre (an Aeolian harp). The music image is eerie: the only song for the dead is mechanical and tidal.

title: mirrors meant to glass the opulent
short: 'Glass' as a verb means to reflect; the mirrors intended to flatter rich passengers now reflect only a sea-worm.
body: 'To glass' (to mirror, reflect an image) is a poetic verb. The first-class saloons were famous for their mirrors and fittings; now 'the sea-worm crawls' over them. The descending string 'grotesque, slimed, dumb, indifferent' moves from the worm's appearance to its moral blankness: 'indifferent' is the key word, for the creature, like the universe of the poem, neither gloats nor pities. The stanza is a version of the vanitas tradition, in which luxury objects are shown overtaken by decay.

sources.cite: Oxford English Dictionary (OED Online)

title: bleared
short: 'Bleared' means dimmed or filmed over, as of eyes; the jewels become sightless eyes in the dark water.
body: To 'blear' is to dim the eyes with rheum or to blur. The jewels, made 'to ravish the sensuous mind' (to transport with delight), lie 'lightless': without light to refract they lose their sparkle. The alliterating triad 'bleared and black and blind' personifies the stones as blinded eyes, preparing for the 'moon-eyed fishes' who gaze back in the next stanza. 'Ravish' carries its older senses of seize and enrapture, with sexual overtones that anticipate the later marriage conceit.

sources.cite: Oxford English Dictionary (OED Online)

title: moon-eyed fishes
short: Deep-sea fish with large round staring eyes, whose naive question is the poem's only speech besides the Spinner's.
body: 'Moon-eyed' means having large, round, staring eyes (and, in an older sense, dim-sighted). The fishes 'gaze at the gilded gear' (gilt fittings) with uncomprehending curiosity, and Hardy gives them a question in deliberately awkward, abstract diction. The comic incongruity of fish speaking Latinate English is part of the satire: human splendour is meaningless to the creatures of the deep. The stanza ends with a printed ellipsis, marking the turn of the poem from present wreck to past history.

sources.cite: Oxford English Dictionary (OED Online)
'The Convergence of the Twain', Wikipedia (summarising Childs, Baldick and Davie)

title: vaingloriousness
short: Boastful, empty pride; the long abstract noun mocks the ship's pretensions in the mouths of fishes.
body: 'Vainglory' (Latin vana gloria, empty glory) is excessive or unwarranted pride in one's achievements, a sin in the medieval scheme closely related to the 'pride of life'. The five-syllable form 'vaingloriousness' is cumbersome on purpose, sitting oddly in the fishes' mouths and making the sentence sound like a moralist's verdict delivered by the wrong speakers. According to the CPRW essay, this fishes' stanza was inserted after the poem's first printing, which ran to thirty lines. Hardy here comes nearest to the sermon on vanity that some critics, such as Donald Davie, find in the poem (Davie reads it as a condemnation of the liner's luxury); others stress that the poem's real subject is cosmic indifference rather than moral punishment.

title: Well: while was fashioning
short: The colloquial 'Well:' marks the turn from the wreck to the history behind it; 'while was fashioning' omits the subject for compression.
body: Stanza VI pivots the poem. After the fishes' question, the speaker answers in a conversational tone ('Well:') and goes back to the period of building in Belfast (the ship was constructed by Harland and Wolff, 1909–12). The syntax is elliptical: 'while [she] was fashioning', or 'while [the Will] was fashioning', the passive-active ambiguity typical of Hardy's crabbed style. The long sentence that begins here runs over three stanzas, the syntax itself enacting the slow, unseen preparation of the meeting. 'Creature of cleaving wing' figures the ship as a bird cutting the air or sea.

title: The Immanent Will
short: Hardy's name, from The Dynasts, for the blind, unconscious force that moves all events in the universe.
body: In The Dynasts (1904–08), Hardy's epic-drama of the Napoleonic wars, the 'Immanent Will' is the unconscious motive power within all things, working without purpose, foresight or feeling; it never speaks, while Spirits (including the Spirit of the Years) comment on its workings. 'Immanent' (Latin immanere, to remain within) distinguishes this force from a transcendent God who acts from outside creation. Hardy's philosophy drew on Schopenhauer's Will and on contemporary science. In this poem the Will 'stirs and urges everything', so that the disaster is neither divine punishment nor pure accident but the working-out of an indifferent process. Critics divide over whether this undercuts the moral reading of stanzas I–V or completes it.

title: sinister mate
short: The iceberg is cast as the ship's destined bride: a marriage conceit carried through 'welding', 'twin halves' and 'consummation'.
body: The central conceit of the second half is a perverse wedding. 'Mate' suggests a spouse; 'sinister' means ominous, and in heraldry 'on the left' (Latin sinister), perhaps a hint of a left-handed, ill-omened match. 'So gaily great' gives the ship a bride's festive splendour. The Iceberg grows 'in shadowy silent distance' as the ship grows 'in stature, grace, and hue', like two partners maturing for an arranged union. 'A Shape of Ice' is deliberately vague and capitalised, almost a spectral figure. 'Dissociate' (separated) contrasts with the 'intimate welding' to come.

title: smart
short: 'Smart' means fashionable and elegant, with a glance at its older sense of sharp or stinging.
body: In 1912 'smart' was a fashionable word for stylish, socially elevated (the 'smart set' who sailed first class). It also retains its original senses, brisk and quick, and, as noun and verb, sharp pain. The colloquial adjective brings the social satire of stanzas I–V into the account of the ship's growth. The paired verbs 'grew … grew' set the ship's construction and the iceberg's formation in exact parallel across a single stanza, the structural core of the poem's design.

sources.cite: Oxford English Dictionary (OED Online)

title: intimate welding
short: A metallurgical metaphor for the collision that is also a sexual and marital one: two bodies fused together.
body: 'Welding' (uniting metal pieces by heat and pressure) suits a steel ship, and the Titanic was in fact riveted rather than welded, so the word is figurative. 'Intimate' adds the sense of close personal, even sexual, union. The phrase 'their later history' treats ship and iceberg as characters in a novel whose plots are converging unseen, a typically Hardyan view of coincidence. No 'mortal eye' could see it: only a perspective outside time, like that of the Spirits in The Dynasts, perceives the pattern.

sources.cite: Oxford English Dictionary (OED Online)

title: anon … august event
short: 'Anon' means soon, by and by; 'august' means majestic or awe-inspiring, used here with deep irony.
body: 'Anon' is an archaism for 'soon' or 'presently'. 'August' (Latin augustus, venerable) gives the collision the dignity of a solemn ceremony, continuing the wedding conceit (a royal or august marriage) while ironically elevating a catastrophe. 'Bent … on' means set upon, determined toward, as if ship and iceberg had intentions; 'paths coincident' uses the geometric sense of coincident (occupying the same place), so that what looks like accident becomes an exact meeting of lines plotted in advance. The irony is that the human builders meant an 'august' maiden voyage, and the Will delivered a different august event.

sources.cite: Oxford English Dictionary (OED Online)

title: the Spinner of the Years
short: A figure of fate, recalling the Greek Fates who spin the thread of life and Hardy's own Spirit of the Years.
body: In Greek myth the three Moirai (Fates) spin, measure and cut each mortal's thread of life; Clotho, the Spinner, is their best-known emblem. Hardy fuses this image with the Spirit of the Years from The Dynasts, the oldest and most detached of the commenting Spirits. The Spinner's single word 'Now!' is the poem's climax: an act of timing rather than of judgement, which supports the reading that the disaster is fated rather than punitive. The sudden direct speech after so much slow syntax enacts the instant of impact.

title: consummation … jars two hemispheres
short: 'Consummation' means completion and also the sexual completion of a marriage; the collision 'jars', shocks, both halves of the world.
body: 'Consummation' completes the marriage conceit: a marriage is legally consummated by sexual union. The word also means completion or end, and it echoes Christ's last word in the Vulgate, 'consummatum est' ('It is finished', John 19:30), and Hamlet's death as 'a consummation devoutly to be wished'. 'Jars two hemispheres' works at several levels: the physical shock of the impact; the news shaking both the Old World and the New, since the ship sailed from Southampton for New York; and perhaps the two halves of a single sphere brought together. Readers disagree whether the ending is a tragic recognition or a sardonic joke at the expense of human pride.
